TOPICS#1.s: Italian is spelled the way it sounds

sec.p: Every letter is pronounced. The vowels are short and clear: a (ah), e (eh), i (ee), o (oh), u (oo). Never glide them like in English.

sec.h: C and G change before e and i
sec.p: Before e or i, c sounds like "ch" and g like "j". Before a, o, u they are hard: k and g. Add an h to keep them hard before e or i.
gn is like "ny" in canyon. gli is like "lli" in million. sc before e or i is "sh". sch is "sk".
Double letters are held longer. It can change the meaning, so listen closely.
Most words are stressed on the second to last syllable (a-MI-co). A written accent shows stress on the last syllable.

sec.p: Most nouns ending in -o are masculine, in -a feminine. Nouns in -e can be either, so learn them with their article.
-o becomes -i. -a becomes -e. -e becomes -i.
-ca and -ga become -che and -ghe to keep the hard sound. -co usually becomes -chi or -ci. Some words never change: nouns ending in an accent, and foreign words.
Italian verbs end in -are, -ere or -ire. Remove the ending to get the stem, then add the endings for each person.
The ending already tells who is acting, so Italians usually drop io, tu, noi... Use them only for emphasis.
ex: Io parlo italiano, lui parla francese.
I speak Italian, he speaks French.

sec.p: Many -ire verbs, like finire, add -isc- in io, tu, lui and loro: finisco, finisci, finisce, finiamo, finite, finiscono.

CULT#1: Italians drink cappuccino at breakfast, not after meals. After lunch or dinner, ask for un caffè, which means an espresso.
Many restaurants add a small cover charge per person, called il coperto. It is normal and is shown on the menu or bill.

Pranzo (lunch) is around 12:30 to 14:00. Cena (dinner) usually starts after 20:00, so restaurants can be empty earlier.

For many regional train paper tickets you must stamp them in the machine on the platform before boarding (convalidare).

sec#1.p: The imperfetto describes what used to happen, what was going on, and how things were. There is no clear start or end.
ex: As a child I used to play football.

sec#1.p: Drop -are, -ere or -ire and add the endings.
Very few verbs are irregular. Essere is fully irregular: ero, eri, era, eravamo, eravate, erano. Fare, dire and bere use the longer stem: facevo, dicevo, bevevo.
ex: As a child I was shy.
I used to have breakfast at seven.

sec#1.p: Use the imperfetto for a habit or an action in progress. Use the passato prossimo for a finished event that interrupts it.
ex: While I was eating, Marco arrived.

sec#2.p: The conditional means would. It is the polite way to ask for things.
ex: I would like a coffee, please.

sec#2.p: Take the future stem and add the endings -ei, -esti, -ebbe, -emmo, -este, -ebbero.
Also use it for things you would like or would do.
ex: I would gladly eat a pizza.

q#2: How do you say "I would like"?
Vorrei is the conditional of volere.

sec#3.p: A direct object pronoun replaces a noun and goes before the conjugated verb.
The participle agrees with the pronoun. Lo and la shorten to l' before a vowel or h.
ex: Ho comprato la pasta. L'ho comprata.
I bought the pasta. I bought it.
Ho visto i ragazzi. Li ho visti.
I saw the boys. I saw them.

sec#3.p: The pronoun can go before the modal verb or join the end of the infinitive.

q#3: Le mele is feminine plural: le.

sec#4.p: Use più (more) and meno (less). Use di before a noun or pronoun, and che between two adjectives, verbs or places.
ex: Roma è più grande di Firenze.
È più facile parlare che scrivere.
It is easier to talk than to write.

sec#4.p: Use come or (tanto) quanto for as ... as.
ex: I am as tall as you.

sec#4.p: A few words have their own comparative.
Add the article before più to say the most.

sec#5.p: Ci replaces a place you already mentioned. Ci is also used in c'è (there is) and ci sono (there are).
ex: Vai a Roma? Sì, ci vado domani.
Are you going to Rome? Yes, I am going there tomorrow.

sec#5.p: Ne replaces a quantity or a part of something. Keep the number after the verb.
ex: Vuoi del pane? Sì, ne voglio un po'.

q: Ragazzo is masculine singular: il ragazzo.
Ragazza is feminine singular: la ragazza.
Before a vowel, masculine plural uses gli.
Masculine singular before s + consonant uses lo.
Feminine singular before a vowel uses l'.

PL_GRAMMAR#1.title: Gender & plurals
q: Amico → amici; the masculine plural drops the h-less soft c spelling.
Amica → amiche; h preserves the hard c sound.

PL_GRAMMAR#1.title: Prepositions
PL_GRAMMAR#1.intro: Use the correct preposition in context.
q: Di can indicate language or subject.
Travel by train is in treno.

PL_GRAMMAR#1.title: Pronouns
PL_GRAMMAR#1.intro: Replace or identify the right personal pronoun.

PL_GRAMMAR#1.title: Negation
PL_GRAMMAR#1.intro: Use non before a conjugated verb.

PL_GRAMMAR#1.title: Past tense

PL_GRAMMAR.push#1.title: Imperfetto
PL_GRAMMAR.push#1.intro: Describe habitual or ongoing past actions.
q: Da bambino, io ___ sempre al parco. (giocare)
L’imperfetto giocavo expresses a habitual past action.
Leggevo describes a simultaneous ongoing past activity.
Quando ero piccolo, ___ paura del buio.
Avevo expresses a state in the past.

PL_GRAMMAR.push#1.title: Condizionale
PL_GRAMMAR.push#1.intro: Make polite requests and express possibilities.
q: Vorrei is a polite conditional request.
Potremmo is conditional present, first-person plural.
Dovresti gives advice in the conditional.
Potresti is a polite second-person conditional.

PL_GRAMMAR.push#1.title: Congiuntivo
q: Penso che often introduces the congiuntivo: abbia.
Spero che commonly takes the subjunctive: stia.

PL_GRAMMAR.push#1.title: Formal register & cohesion
PL_GRAMMAR.push#1.intro: Select precise structures for formal Italian.
q: Most formal opening for a business email:
Gentile + title/surname is a conventional formal salutation.
Formal alternative to «però» in an argument:
Tuttavia is a formal adversative connector.
Nonostante introduces a contrast; the main clause requires a finite predicate.
Resto a disposizione per ulteriori chiarimenti.
A formal business closing should match the register.

PL_GRAMMAR.push#1.title: Nuance & idiomatic meaning
PL_GRAMMAR.push#1.intro: Interpret advanced idioms and rhetorical nuance.
q: «Prendere due piccioni con una fava» means:
ottenere due risultati con una sola azione
The idiom means achieving two aims with one action.
A malincuore means reluctantly or with regret.
«In fin dei conti» is closest to:
The expression introduces a final consideration.
la possibilità che qualcosa non accada
Non è detto che expresses uncertainty, often followed by the subjunctive.
